adversarial_test_results.prompt:
Rivers carry sediment from the mountains to the sea. Every spring the meltwater lifts grains of sand and stone from the upper valleys and carries them downstream, where the current slows and the load settles onto the bed. Over many centuries these deposits build broad flats that flood each year and then drain again, leaving behind layers of silt that farmers have learned to read like the pages of a book.

The colour of a river tells you something about what it carries. Clear water running over granite looks almost green in the shade, while a river swollen by rain turns the colour of weak tea as the mud spreads through it. Fish move up the tributaries when the water warms, and the birds that hunt them follow the same route a few weeks later.

People who live along a river learn its moods. A stream that barely covers the ankles in August can tear out a bridge in April. The old houses in the valley stand on raised ground for a reason, and the marks painted on the stone walls record the height of floods that nobody now alive remembers.

The water itself is only part of the story. A river shapes the land it crosses, cutting a channel through soft rock and bending around the harder beds. Where the slope is steep the channel is narrow and fast; where the valley opens out, the river spreads into a wide, slow sheet that drops its load and splits into smaller channels. These channels shift from year to year, so a map of the delta drawn a generation ago no longer matches the ground.

Many towns grew up where a river could be crossed. The first bridges were timber and were washed away more than once; the stone ones that replaced them still carry traffic today. Weirs built to hold back the water still stand, though the wheels they once turned are long gone.

Careful study of a single river can take a lifetime. Gauges record the height of the water every hour, samples are taken to measure what the water carries, and photographs from the same viewpoint, year after year, show how the banks have moved. The records are dull to read, but they are the only way to tell a slow change from a passing flood.

In 1998 the heritage directorate approved a plan to restore the old channel, and the work that followed uncovered timbers that had lain under the mud for two hundred years. Volunteers cleaned and recorded each piece before the water was let back in.
